overview: Nine Entertainment is Australia's largest locally-owned media company, operating free-to-air television (Channel 9, 9Now) and the Stan subscription streaming service under a combined Streaming & Broadcast segment, a Publishing division of masthead newspapers and digital marketplaces (The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, Australian Financial Review, Drive), and, since completing the $850m acquisition of QMS Media on 31 March 2026, a digital Outdoor (out-of-home) advertising business. In FY26 Nine divested its 60% stake in Domain Holdings (sold to CoStar Group for cash proceeds of $1,680.5m), Nine Radio, Pedestrian Group and its stake in Future Women, and converted its regional NBN (Northern NSW) and Nine Darwin television operations to affiliate arrangements with WIN Network, materially reshaping the portfolio toward streaming, digital publishing and outdoor.

business_model.summary: Nine is primarily an advertising-funded media business (television spot advertising, digital display/video, outdoor/out-of-home media and classified/marketplace advertising) layered with a growing base of recurring subscription revenue from Stan streaming and digital news subscriptions, plus emerging AI content-licensing deals. Free-to-air TV advertising is cyclical and transactional; Stan and digital subscriptions are recurring; Outdoor (QMS) is contracted media-space revenue with growing programmatic/digital components; Publishing blends print advertising decline with growing digital subscription, marketplace (Drive) and licensing revenue.
business_model.customer_type: B2C advertising-funded (advertisers are the paying customer; audiences/subscribers are the product) plus direct B2C subscriptions (Stan, digital news) and growing B2B data/content-licensing deals (e.g., Microsoft Copilot, corporate AI licensing)
business_model.geographic_mix: Overwhelmingly Australia-domestic; QMS also has a New Zealand outdoor media presence (QMS NZ).

main_competitors: News Corp Australia (The Australian, Foxtel, Kayo)
Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, Binge/Foxtel (streaming)
Google, Meta, YouTube, TikTok (digital/video advertising dollars)
ARN Media/Southern Cross Austereo (radio, now divested by Nine)
competitive_position.market_position: Nine is the leading Australian commercial free-to-air broadcaster by audience share (reported ~42.8% share of Total Television revenue among the three major commercial networks for FY26, in a market that declined ~9.6%), Stan is the only Australian-owned subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) service and a clear #2/3 player behind Netflix, and QMS is the #3 player in Australian out-of-home advertising behind oOh!media and JCDecaux. Nine's mastheads (SMH, The Age, AFR) are leading premium news brands.

moat_factors.description: Integrated Consumer Platform links TV, Stan, Publishing and now Outdoor audience data, enabling cross-platform ad targeting and 'Sofa to Street' advertiser propositions that smaller single-platform rivals cannot match.

Long-dated rights to NRL (through 2034, though shared with Foxtel), State of Origin, NRL Grand Final, Australian Open, and Stan Sport's Premier League rights drive appointment viewing and subscriber retention.
SMH, The Age and AFR are leading premium news brands with monetizable archives, now being licensed to AI platforms (Microsoft Copilot) and corporates.
FTA broadcast licences and spectrum allocation limit new free-to-air entrants; News Media Bargaining Incentive legislation is pushing global platforms to pay for content.
Stan's 'only Australian-owned' status is a marketing differentiator but does not match the content budgets of Netflix or Disney.

weaknesses: Structurally declining linear FTA TV advertising market (Total TV EBITDA fell 12% in FY26; a $404m non-cash impairment was taken against Total TV's carrying value)

Lost the bulk of pay/streaming NRL rights value to Foxtel in the July 2026 renewal (Nine retained free-to-air/BVOD rights to Origin, Grand Final and limited live matches; Foxtel pays the much larger share of the $5.3bn total deal)
Heavily domestic, single-market (Australia) concentration with no major international diversification
Integration risk and execution risk from simultaneously absorbing QMS while divesting five other businesses in one year
Scale still far below global streaming and digital-advertising platforms (Netflix, Google, Meta) that compete for the same attention and ad dollars

growth_drivers: QMS Outdoor integration: targeted ~$20m cost synergies over three years plus revenue synergies from the 'Sofa to Street' cross-platform advertiser proposition; QMS pro forma FY26 EBITDA grew >18% and management guides to double-digit EBITDA growth in FY27

Stan subscriber and ARPU growth, driven by Premier League/Stan Sport content, a new August 2026 ad-supported tier on Stan Entertainment, and advertising on Stan Sport, alongside ~2.3m paying subscribers as at August 2026

Digital Publishing growth: digital subscription/licensing revenue +11% in FY26, Drive marketplace revenue +27% (dealer listings +94% YoY), and new AI content-licensing deals (Microsoft Copilot, banking/mining corporates) creating a new high-margin revenue stream

Nine2028 cost transformation program: delivered $105m of cost-out in FY26 against a target raised to more than $160m (reported elsewhere as raised to $180m) of cumulative efficiencies through FY27, extended beyond 2028
Portfolio rebalancing toward growth: management guides to ~70% of FY27 EBITDA (~60% of revenue) coming from Streaming, Digital Publishing and Outdoor rather than legacy linear TV/radio/print
Long-dated NRL rights secured through 2034 (State of Origin, Grand Final, NRLW, weekly matches) underpinning live-sport audience and subscriber value for FTA and Stan
AI-driven efficiency and new monetization: Gemini rollout across six functional areas, content-licensing deals, and in-house LLM-grounding agreements

business.risk: Secular decline in linear FTA TV advertising
business.description: Total Television revenue fell materially (ex-Olympics down 2%) in a TV ad market that KPMG data shows declined 9.6% in FY26; a $404m impairment was booked against the Total TV cash-generating unit.

business.risk: Loss of bulk NRL rights value to Foxtel
business.description: The July 2026 seven-year, $5.3bn NRL deal saw Foxtel take the lion's share (~$520m/yr) of rights including most live matches and streaming, while Nine pays ~$145-150m/yr for FTA exclusivity on Origin, the Grand Final and limited matches — commentary described Nine's broader NRL-streaming ambitions as curtailed.

Nine simultaneously integrated a large debt-funded acquisition (QMS) while divesting Domain, Nine Radio, Pedestrian, Future Women and restructuring regional TV in the same year; cost-synergy and revenue-synergy targets are not yet proven.

business.risk: Intensifying competition for audience and ad dollars
business.description: Global streaming platforms (Netflix, Disney+, Amazon) and digital advertising platforms (Google, Meta, YouTube, TikTok) compete directly for both viewing attention and advertiser budgets, structurally pressuring Nine's legacy FTA and Publishing display revenue.

financial.description: Net debt rose to $658m at 30 June 2026 (from $451m a year earlier) and net leverage rose to 1.7x EBITDA (from 1.4x), reflecting debt funding of the $850m QMS acquisition net of Domain sale proceeds already distributed via the $777m special dividend.

Management has flagged that near-term ordinary dividends will be unfranked given the timing of the Domain sale tax position and other transactions, reducing the after-tax yield for domestic shareholders relying on franking credits.

financial.risk: Cash tax including CGT on Domain sale
financial.description: FY26 cash tax paid, inclusive of capital gains tax on the Domain sale, was $241m, a one-off but material cash outflow in the transition year.

regulatory.description: Outcomes of the News Media Bargaining Incentive and ongoing negotiations with AI platforms over use of Nine's journalism are still being finalised; some AI platforms are lobbying to weaken Australian copyright protections, per the Chair's letter.

regulatory.risk: Commercial Broadcasting Tax and spectrum policy
regulatory.description: The government has suspended the Commercial Broadcasting Tax for a further two years, but formal consultation on future broadcast services and spectrum demand ahead of the 2030s could change the economics of FTA broadcasting.

regulatory.risk: General media regulation (content, privacy, defamation, industrial awards)
regulatory.description: Ongoing exposure to changes in FTA licence conditions, advertising restrictions, privacy law reform and defamation law interpretation.

macro.description: Nine's core revenue (FTA, digital display, outdoor) is highly correlated with Australian GDP, consumer and business confidence; a soft advertising market was repeatedly cited as a FY26 headwind across all segments.

macro.risk: Interest rate sensitivity via higher net debt
macro.description: Increased net debt (1.7x leverage) post-QMS makes earnings more sensitive to Australian interest rate movements.

Content costs (sports rights, programming), wage inflation, and QMS's outdoor operating costs (fuel/petrol-dependent logistics, site leases) are exposed to general cost inflation, partly offset by structural cost-out programs.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian TV advertising is a mature, structurally declining market (down ~9.6% in FY26 per KPMG data) being replaced by digital video, streaming subscription, and out-of-home/digital-outdoor advertising, which are growing faster; AI-driven content licensing is an emerging, still-small revenue opportunity for premium publishers.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — advertising revenue (TV, publishing display, outdoor) is discretionary and closely tracks the broader Australian economic/consumer-spending cycle; subscription revenue (Stan, digital news) is more resilient and recurring.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — net debt of $658m and 1.7x leverage at 30 June 2026 following the debt-funded QMS acquisition increases sensitivity to RBA rate settings, though the balance sheet remains well within covenant levels.
key_input_costs: Sports and content rights (NRL, AFL-adjacent, Premier League, Olympics)
Outdoor site leases and digital screen hardware
Fuel/logistics costs for QMS physical network

recent_developments.event: Completed the sale of Nine's 60% stake in Domain Holdings to CoStar Group for cash proceeds of $1,680.5m (gain on sale after tax of $670m); funded a $777m fully franked special dividend (49 cents/share) paid 26 September 2025.

Agreed (30 Jan 2026) and completed (31 Mar 2026) the ~$850m acquisition of QMS Media (digital outdoor advertising) from Quadrant Private Equity, adding a fast-growing, >95%-digital-revenue Outdoor segment.

Completed the sale of Nine's broadcast radio assets (2GB, 3AW, 4BC, 6PR, 2UE, Magic1278, 4BH) on a cash-and-debt-free enterprise value of $56m, and sold Pedestrian Group and its stake in Future Women.

Converted regional television assets NBN (Northern NSW) and Nine Darwin from wholly-owned operations to affiliate arrangements with WIN Network, effective 2 June 2026, receiving $20.5m cash consideration.

Secured NRL and NRLW broadcast rights through to 2034 as part of a seven-year, $5.3bn industry-wide deal with Foxtel and Sky NZ; Nine retains free-to-air/BVOD exclusivity on State of Origin, the Grand Final, NRLW and a limited number of weekly matches for an estimated ~$145-150m/year, while Foxtel secured the larger share of live-match and streaming rights.

Signed an Australian-first content-licensing agreement with Microsoft's CoPilot to allow referencing of Nine's masthead journalism, plus licensing deals with major Australian banking and mining corporates for use of publishing archives in internal LLMs.

Reported FY26 results (year to 30 June 2026): continuing-business revenue $2.2bn (+3%), Group EBITDA $379m (+17%), NPATA $147m (+11%), statutory net profit $511m (including $849m after-tax profit from discontinued operations, largely the Domain gain), partly offset by a $404m non-cash impairment of the Total TV segment; announced an interim/final ordinary dividend of 7.5 cents per share for FY26 plus the earlier 49-cent special dividend.

Leadership transition: Matthew Stanton confirmed as permanent CEO (March 2025) after acting in the role; Catherine West stepped down as Chair at the November 2025 AGM and was succeeded by Peter Tonagh (former News Corp Australia and Foxtel CEO).

items.target: ~70% of Group EBITDA (and ~60% of revenue) from Streaming, Digital Publishing and Outdoor
items.notes: Reflects the post-restructure portfolio including a full year of QMS versus only one quarter in FY26.

items.target: More than $160m cumulative efficiencies over three years to FY27 (some trade press reports this target subsequently raised to ~$180m)
items.notes: FY26 delivered $105m (or >$60m recurring cost-out cited elsewhere) in-year; management says the program is tracking ahead of plan and has been extended beyond 2028.
Builds on >18% pro forma EBITDA growth for QMS in FY26 and the Metcash retail-format partnership starting September 2026.

items.target: 60-80% of Net Profit After Tax before Specific Items, excluding acquisition-related intangible amortisation (NPATA)
items.notes: Near-term dividends flagged as unfranked given the timing of recent transactions (Domain sale tax position, QMS acquisition funding).
Management expects the Total TV advertising market to remain challenging, with cost discipline offsetting continued revenue softness.
No specific dollar figure given; new AI-licensing deals (Microsoft CoPilot, corporate partners) are incremental upside not yet quantified in guidance.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Matt Stanton described FY26 as 'a defining period' marked by high-conviction portfolio reshaping (QMS acquisition funded by Domain, Radio, Pedestrian and regional TV divestments) and said the newly aligned portfolio has 'significant potential' to grow further, citing resilience and growth in Stan, Digital Publishing and Outdoor against a 'challenging advertising market' for Total TV. Chair Peter Tonagh emphasised disciplined capital allocation (the $777m special dividend, QMS's long-dated leased asset base, continued 60-80% payout policy) and highlighted AI content-licensing deals and the NRL rights renewal as proof that 'Australian content has worth.'

bull_case: Portfolio has been decisively rebalanced toward structurally growing segments (Stan streaming, digital publishing, digital outdoor) which are guided to deliver ~70% of FY27 EBITDA, reducing reliance on the declining linear TV ad market

QMS acquisition adds a high-margin, >95%-digital-revenue outdoor business with identified cost synergies (~$20m) and strong organic growth (pro forma EBITDA +18% in FY26), creating a unique cross-platform 'Sofa to Street' advertiser proposition

Stan delivered record FY26 growth (revenue +16%, EBITDA +34%) as the only Australian-owned SVOD service, with a new ad-supported tier and Premier League/Stan Sport content driving subscriber and ARPU growth

Emerging AI content-licensing revenue stream (Microsoft CoPilot and corporate deals) monetizes Nine's journalism archives at high margin, and the Nine2028 cost program is tracking ahead of its savings targets

Simplified, deleveraged focus following the Domain/Radio/Pedestrian divestments returned substantial capital to shareholders ($777m special dividend) while securing long-dated NRL rights (to 2034) for key free-to-air sport franchises
bear_case: Core linear FTA TV advertising remains in structural decline (market down ~9.6% in FY26, Total TV EBITDA down 12%, with a $404m non-cash impairment taken against the segment) and this still represents the largest single revenue pool

Nine ceded the bulk of the lucrative NRL streaming and live-match rights to Foxtel in the July 2026 renewal, retaining only free-to-air exclusivity on marquee fixtures — a setback for its broader sports-streaming ambitions on Stan

Net debt and leverage rose materially (to $658m / 1.7x EBITDA) to fund the debt-financed QMS acquisition, adding integration risk just as the group also divested five other businesses in the same year

Near-term dividends are unfranked, reducing after-tax returns for domestic shareholders, and advertising-market cyclicality leaves earnings exposed to any further softening in Australian consumer/business confidence

Structural competition from global streaming platforms (Netflix, Disney+) and digital-advertising giants (Google, Meta, YouTube) continues to compress both audience attention and ad pricing power across Nine's legacy FTA and Publishing businesses
